chapter.title: Introduction
chapter.para: This document provides information about spectra saved to HDF5 formatted files. Starting with SpecTcl 7.0-005, swrite and sread support -format hdf5 which allows spectrum to be written to HDF5 formatted files. HDF5 iteslf is beyond the scope of this document. For information about HDF5, see .

This document is intended for people who want to make use of spectra stored in HDF5 files outside of SpecTcl. A specTcl installation will have this document in html format in $SPECTCLHOME/share/hdf5/index.html where $SPECTCLHOME is the top level of the installation directory.

SpecTcl provies a low level library libhdfReader that contains a C++ class that can extract information about and the contents of spectra that are stored in those files. The remainder of this document is organized as follows:

listitem.para: Describes the compilation and link options you'll need to supply to use this library in your programs.

Works through an example program that makes use of the library. This program, and the sample data file are available in $SPECTCLHOME/share/hdf5example where $SPECTCLHOME is the top level directory of a SpecTcl instalation.
Provides information that describes how the HDF5 is structured. You will need to have a basic understanding of the objects that can live in an HDF5 file to understand this information.

chapter.title: Looking at a sample program
chapter.para: This section works through a simple program that uses the hdfReader API. The program iself is installed in $SPECTCLHOME/share/hdf5example/listample.cpp. It opens a sample HDF5 data file from its working directory and exercises the HDF5 spectrum API. The sample data file is $SPECTCLHOME/share/hdf5example/sample.hdf.

example.title: Sample libhdfReader program

chapter.para: In the discussion below, refer to the numbered callouts in the example above for the corresponding code.

callout.para: Inludes the header that defines the hdfSpectrumReader class which provides support for reading the SpecTcl swrite -format hdf5 .

Creating an instance of the hdfSpectruReader, opens the file path passed to it as an HDF5 file readonly. When the object is destroyed, its destructor will close that HDF5 file. The methods of this object will provide access to the objects that are stored in the file.

The objects in the HDF5 file are associated with spectra. Each spectrum stored in the file has a name, the name of that spectrum in SpecTcl if swrite -format hdf5 was used to write it. The listSpectra method returns a vector of strings that provide the names of the spectra that are stored in the file.

The program is going to iterate over the names gotten from listSpectra and operate on each spectrum in turn. If you are not familiar with this form of the C++ for loop, it iterates over all elements of a collection that supports generating iterators with betin and end and for each iteration, in this case, the variable n is assigned to one of the values in the collection.
For a more complete description of this so-called range-based for loop you can see

Each SpecTcl spectrum has a channel data type. The dataType method takes a spectrum name for a spetrum that is in the file and provides it's data type string. For SpecTcl this is a string containing one of:

While SpecTcl provides 1-D and 2-D spectra, its spectra also describe how events increment them in a very rich way. The spectrumType takes a spectrum name and returns a string that defines the spectrum type. For a list of spectrum types supported by SpecTcl, see the spectrum reference in the
SpecTcl Command reference

Since SpecTcl spectra are fundamentally 1-D or 2-D data, they may have one or two axis definitions. An axis definition describes a mapping between parameter space and the bins of a spectrum. The getXaxis returns the X axis definition of a the spectrum whose name was passed to it. All Spectra have an X axis definition. The axis definition is returned as a struct (hdf5SpectrumReader::AxisDefinition). With the following fields:

listitem.para: The low limit of parameter space represented by the axis.
The high limit of parameter space represented by the axis.
The number of bins on the axis.

callout.para: While all spectra have an X axis, only those that are fundamentally 2-d have Y axes. The hasYAxis when passed the name of a spectrum returns true if that spectrum has a Y axis, false if not.
If a specturm has a Y axis it is safe to invoke getYaxis which returns its axis definition.

The getParameters retuns a list of the names of parameters for the spectrum, but see, however getYParameters below. In many cases, a 2-d spectrum's parameter can be described by a single list, for example, a simple 2-d spectrum's X parameter will be the first in the list and the Y parameter, the second.

Some spectrum types are not unambiguosyl defined by a single list of parameters. For example the Gamma Deluxe (gd) spectrum has a set of X axis parameters and a set of Y axis parameters and increments for any pair of those that are present. It is best described by a pair of parameter lists. The hasYparameters returns true if there is a second parameter list for the spectrum. That second set of parameters is returned from getYParameters.

All SpecTcl spectra have a gate applied to it. When created, the spectrum's gate is called -TRUE- and is true for all events. Subsequently, more intereting gates can be created and applied to the spectrum. The getGate returns the name of the gate that was applied to the spetrum at the time the file was created.

Spectra can have arbitrary metadata associated with them. Spectrum metadata is simply a set of name/value pairs where both the name and the value are strings. The getMetadata returns the metadata for a spectrum as an std::vector<std::pair<std::string std::string>>. Each pair is a metadata item. the first element of the pair is the name of that metadata item and the second element of the pair is the value of that metadata item.

Finally, and maybe most importantly, the contents of the spectra can be retrieved from file. The result of a call to getContents is a pointer to dynmamically allocated storage which contains the contents of the spectrum saved to file. Note how the code blow the call to getContents uses the data type string returned from dataType to create the appropriate pointer type. In our simple example, we just then free the storage allocated by getContents.
What you do with spectrum contents is so application specific that we leave that completely up to you.
